location: Task 2, Step 3, `allocate()` loop (plan lines 529-561) and the Produces contract (lines 320-324). Task 5 (line 680) says OrdersService writes the `OrderLineAllocation` rows.
title: allocate() moves stock and writes ORDER_OUT but never writes the OrderLineAllocation rows that release() and delivery read
failure_scenario: The batch decrement and the ledger row happen inside AllocationService. The reservation record is left to Task 5, which has to map `AllocationResult` back to order lines by `itemId` alone, because `AllocationRequest` has no orderLineId. Suppose Task 5 skips or mis-maps the rows for one line: line X gets 200 units allocated but no row is written. Warehouse cache and ledger both show -200, so they agree and ledger-assert stays silent. Delivery credits the client 0 for that line. A cancel at CONFIRMED runs release(), whose findMany returns [], so nothing is restored and the 200 units are lost. Task 7's test 'restores exactly the allocated quantities' still passes, since it compares against the missing rows (0 == 0). OrderLine has no @@unique([orderId, itemId]), so two lines for the same item would be merged under one itemId key. The Task 2 release test depends on an undefined helper `confirmAnOrderFor()` that has to re-implement Task 5's row writing, so it tests the helper and not production code.
fix: Make the decrement, the ledger movement and the reservation one code path. Add `orderLineId: string` to AllocationRequest. In the loop, right after stockMovement.create, add `await tx.orderLineAllocation.create({ data: { orderLineId: request.orderLineId, batchId: batch.id, qtyUnits: take } })`. Key the results by orderLineId. In Task 1 add `@@unique([orderId, itemId])` to OrderLine. Add a Task 2 test asserting that after allocate, SUM(order_line_allocations.qtyUnits) for the order equals minus the SUM of ORDER_OUT qtyUnitsDelta for refId = orderId.

location: Task 2, Step 3, `release()` (lines 583-618), and the `allocate()` contract (lines 323, 488-495: 'must be called inside a transaction' is the only precondition).
title: No per-order exclusion: concurrent double release, double confirm, or cancel racing deliver creates stock silently
failure_scenario: release() reads allocations with a plain findMany, increments batches, then runs deleteMany. Take a double-tapped cancel (or two admins cancelling) on one CONFIRMED order. Tx1 and Tx2 both run findMany before Tx1 commits, and both see the 200-unit allocation. Tx2's `increment` waits on Tx1's row lock. Under READ COMMITTED it then re-applies `qty = qty + 200` to the committed row, and its deleteMany quietly matches 0 rows. Concrete numbers: batch received 500; order A took 200 (300 left); order B took 300 (0 left). A double release of A gives 0 + 200 + 200 = 400. That is at most 500, so warehouse_batches_qty_sane passes. The ledger reads +500 -200 -300 +200 +200 = 400 and agrees with the cache, so ledger-assert is silent, but only 200 units exist. The same shape applies to two concurrent confirms of one PLACED order: allocate runs twice, stock is decremented twice, allocation rows are doubled, and delivery credits the client twice. It also applies to cancel(RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE) racing deliver: the warehouse is restored and the client is credited. Task 5's 'confirming twice is refused' and Task 7's 'cancelling twice is refused' are sequential tests and cannot catch any of this.
fix: (1) Add a header rule: every order transition begins with a conditional update that takes the order row lock, `const { count } = await tx.order.updateMany({ where: { id, status: from }, data: { status: to, ... } }); if (count !== 1) throw CONFLICT;`, and this happens BEFORE calling allocate/release. Under READ COMMITTED the loser re-evaluates `status = from` after the winner commits and gets count 0. (2) Make release() idempotent by construction. Delete first and restore only what was actually deleted: `const rows = await tx.$queryRaw<{ batchId: string; qtyUnits: number; itemId: string }[]>` with SQL `DELETE FROM "order_line_allocations" a USING "order_lines" l WHERE a."orderLineId" = l.id AND l."orderId" = ${orderId} RETURNING a."batchId", a."qtyUnits", l."itemId"`, then increment and write movements per returned row. A concurrent second DELETE blocks on the row locks, finds the rows gone after the first commit, and restores nothing. (3) In allocate, after locking, assert that no allocation rows already exist for opts.orderId. (4) Add concurrent tests: Promise.all of two release() calls on one order must restore exactly once, and two concurrent confirms must leave exactly one set of allocations.

location: Task 2, Step 1, tests 'allocates the earliest-expiring batch first' (lines 331-340) and 'spans batches when one is not enough' (lines 342-353): `seedBatch({ batchNumber: 'EARLY', expiryDays: 30, ... })` against `"expiryDate" > ${cutoff}` with the default minShelfLifeOnDeliveryDays = 30.
title: The plan's own FEFO tests put the EARLY batch exactly on the strict shelf-life boundary, so Step 4 cannot pass as written
failure_scenario: This is separate from known issue (b). The cutoff is now + 30 days. Prisma 7 raw queries send a Date as the text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm' in UTC (adapter-pg mapArg/formatDateTime, with no dbType for raw args). PostgreSQL types it as `date` because of the comparison, and date input drops the time. If seedBatch stores `new Date(Date.now() + 30*86400000)` in the @db.Date column, Prisma writes the same UTC calendar date. `D > D` is false, so EARLY is excluded. 'earliest first' then gets LATE as allocated[0], and 'spans batches' gets [{LATE, 350}] instead of [{EARLY,200},{LATE,150}]. Both fail deterministically. If seedBatch builds a Baghdad-local date instead, they pass only between 00:00 and 03:00 Baghdad time. Step 4 says 'Expected: PASS', so the executor is pushed toward the wrong fix: changing `>` to `>=`, which breaks spec §7.3 (`expiryDate > today + minShelfLife`), or adjusting the helper until the boundary bug is hidden. 'skips a batch with insufficient shelf life' uses 10 vs 300 days, so it cannot tell `>` from `>=` and cannot detect (b).
fix: Move the ordering tests off the boundary: EARLY at 60 days and LATE at 300. Add explicit boundary tests with expiry computed as a business-timezone calendar date string: today_Baghdad + 30 must be excluded and today_Baghdad + 31 must be included. Run both with `vi.setSystemTime` pinned to 22:30 Baghdad (19:30Z) and to 01:30 Baghdad (22:30Z the previous day), so the known (b) off-by-one fails a test. Define `seedBatch` in the plan, going through BatchesService.receive so that a PURCHASE_IN movement exists, which the 'ledger still sums to the cache' test (lines 389-403) requires.

location: Task 2, Step 1, 'TWO CONCURRENT allocations never oversell one batch' (lines 405-434) and Step 5 (lines 627-633). This extends known issue (a).
title: Concurrency test only asserts upper bounds under allSettled, so it passes when either transaction throws or allocates nothing; needs a barrier-based rewrite
failure_scenario: Beyond (a), where the CHECK rejects B and allSettled swallows it: every assertion is an upper bound (`>= 0`, `<= 300`, `sum <= 300`), and rejected promises are simply filtered out. The test therefore also passes if both transactions fail with a deadlock (40P01, which adapter-pg maps to TransactionWriteConflict/P2034), if both hit Prisma's 5 s interactive timeout (defaults verified in the runtime: maxWait 2000, timeout 5000), if pool starvation hits, or if an implementation returns 0 allocated whenever there is contention. It never asserts the correct READ COMMITTED outcome with FOR UPDATE: B blocks, EvalPlanQual re-reads the locked row, and B gets exactly 100 with shortBy 100. The two $transaction calls do take separate pool connections (PrismaPgAdapter.startTransaction calls pool.connect(), and the pg Pool max is 10), so they are not serialized. Whether they overlap is still only timing-dependent, since each tx is about 4 round trips.
fix: Hold A open on a barrier and make B's outcome exact. Sketch: `let locked!: () => void; const aLocked = new Promise<void>(r => (locked = r)); let open!: () => void; const gate = new Promise<void>(r => (open = r)); const a = prisma.$transaction(async tx => { const r = await allocation.allocate(tx, [{ itemId, qtyUnits: 200 }], optsA); locked(); await gate; return r; }, { timeout: 20_000, isolationLevel: 'ReadCommitted' }); await aLocked; const b = prisma.$transaction(tx => allocation.allocate(tx, [{ itemId, qtyUnits: 200 }], optsB), { timeout: 20_000, isolationLevel: 'ReadCommitted' }); await vi.waitFor(async () => { const [w] = await prisma.$queryRaw<{ n: number }[]>` with SQL `SELECT count(*)::int AS n FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database() AND wait_event_type = 'Lock' AND btrim(query) ILIKE 'select%warehouse_batches%'`; `expect(w.n).toBe(1); }); open(); const [ra, rb] = await Promise.all([a, b]); expect(ra[0]).toMatchObject({ qtyUnitsAllocated: 200, shortBy: 0 }); expect(rb[0]).toMatchObject({ qtyUnitsAllocated: 100, shortBy: 100 });` and assert the batch ends at 0. The `::int` cast is needed because count(*) is bigint and would come back as a BigInt. Without FOR UPDATE, B's SELECT does not wait; B instead waits in its UPDATE, so the waitFor fails. After the gate opens, B computes 100 - 200 and hits the 23514 CHECK, so Promise.all rejects. The test then fails deterministically, which is what Step 5 requires.

location: Task 2, Step 3: `for (const request of requests)` with a per-item `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (lines 511-527), including the comment claiming the ORDER BY prevents deadlock. `release()` updates batches in unordered findMany order (lines 588-597). Header rule 1 (line 25).
title: Lock order is only total within one item; multi-item confirmations and releases deadlock
failure_scenario: Confirmation T1 has lines [X, Y] and T2 has [Y, X]. T1 locks X's batches and T2 locks Y's. T1's SELECT for Y waits on T2, and T2's SELECT for X waits on T1. After deadlock_timeout (1 s), PostgreSQL aborts one with 40P01, which surfaces as Prisma P2034, and that admin gets a 500. release() does the same: findMany has no orderBy, and it increments batches in allocation/request order, so a cancel of [X,Y] deadlocks against a confirm of [Y,X]. Phase 5's expiry write-off will be another writer of qtyUnitsRemaining with no stated lock protocol. The ORDER BY comment gives a false assurance, and rule 3 ('every concurrency claim gets a test') is not applied to it.
fix: Lock all items in a single statement with one global order, and have release use the same ORDER BY. In allocate: `const itemIds = [...new Set(requests.map(r => r.itemId))];` then one $queryRaw with `SELECT id, "itemId", "qtyUnitsRemaining" FROM "warehouse_batches" WHERE "itemId" = ANY(${itemIds}) AND "expiryDate" > ${cutoff} ORDER BY "itemId", "expiryDate", "receivedAt", id FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, then group the rows per item in JS, keeping their order. In release, before incrementing: `SELECT id FROM "warehouse_batches" WHERE id = ANY(${batchIds}) ORDER BY "itemId", "expiryDate", "receivedAt", id FOR NO KEY UPDATE`. Reword rule 1 to cover this: every writer of warehouse_batches.qtyUnitsRemaining locks through this ordering. Add a deterministic test: A = tx { allocate([X]); barrier; allocate([Y]) } and B = allocate([Y, X]); wait until B is blocked, open the barrier, and require both to fulfil.

location: Task 2, Step 3, the SQL `... ORDER BY "expiryDate" ASC, "receivedAt" ASC, id ASC FOR UPDATE` (line 526).
title: FOR UPDATE conflicts with the FOR KEY SHARE locks that FK checks take, so deliveries block behind confirmations and can deadlock with them
failure_scenario: Any INSERT that references a warehouse_batches row takes FOR KEY SHARE on that row during the FK check. That covers Task 6's ClientBatchHolding insert and its DELIVERY_IN movement with batchId set, and Phase 4 CLIENT movements with batchId. FOR KEY SHARE conflicts only with FOR UPDATE. Example: delivery D of order O1 inserts a holding for B1 (key-share on B1). Confirmation C of O2 FOR-UPDATE-locks B2, then requests B1 and waits on D. D then inserts the holding for B2 and waits on C. That is a 40P01 deadlock, and one of deliver or confirm fails. Allocate only updates the non-key column qtyUnitsRemaining, and its own UPDATE takes only FOR NO KEY UPDATE, so the stronger lock buys nothing.
fix: Use `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` instead of `FOR UPDATE`. It still conflicts with itself and with UPDATE, so two allocations still serialize on a batch and the oversell protection is unchanged. It does not conflict with FK key-share checks. Update the Step 5 wording to match ('remove the row lock clause').

location: Task 2, Produces (line 323: 'it takes the transaction client ... and will not open its own') and the `allocate(tx: Prisma.TransactionClient, ...)` signature (line 502).
title: 'Must be called inside a transaction' is not enforced: PrismaService type-checks as Prisma.TransactionClient, and in autocommit FOR UPDATE protects nothing
failure_scenario: Prisma.TransactionClient is `Omit<PrismaClient, '$connect'|'$disconnect'|'$on'|'$use'|'$extends'>` (verified in the generated .prisma/client typings; in 7.10 `$transaction` is not denied). So `allocation.allocate(this.prisma, ...)` compiles. In autocommit mode each statement is its own transaction, and the FOR UPDATE locks are released as soon as the SELECT returns. Example for a two-item order: item X's decrement and ORDER_OUT commit; item Y's decrement then fails (CHECK or error). X's units are gone, against an order that is still PLACED and has no allocation rows, so release can never restore them. Ledger and cache agree, and nothing flags it.
fix: Add a runtime guard at the top of allocate and release: `if (typeof (tx as { $connect?: unknown }).$connect === 'function') throw new Error('AllocationService requires an interactive-transaction client');`. The ITX client strips $connect: in the runtime, the removeProperties helper makes `has` return false and the value undefined. Add a test that `allocation.allocate(prisma, ...)` rejects and writes nothing.

location: Task 1, Step 3, constraint `orders_cancel_disposition_required` (lines 290-296) and its comment 'A cancelled order that was ever allocated must say where the goods went'.
title: Disposition CHECK is both stricter and weaker than the §7.4 rule; it allows the exact ambiguity it claims to remove
failure_scenario: The CHECK requires a disposition for every CANCELLED order, including PLACED and CONFIRMED cancels, where Task 7's rules say `dispositionRequired: false` and the client cancel endpoint takes no disposition. A Task 7 implementation writing `cancelDisposition: dto.disposition ?? null` therefore gets a 23514 and a 500. The obvious patch, `?? 'NOT_ALLOCATED'`, satisfies the CHECK everywhere. That includes an OUT_FOR_DELIVERY cancel whose disposition validation is buggy or missing: it is stored as NOT_ALLOCATED, no stock movement is written, and the goods are effectively written off with the record saying they were never allocated. The database accepts it. The plan also never says which disposition a CONFIRMED cancel stores.
fix: Tie the disposition to lifecycle timestamps that the database can see. Replace the CHECK with: `CHECK (("status" <> 'CANCELLED' AND "cancelDisposition" IS NULL) OR ("status" = 'CANCELLED' AND "cancelledAt" IS NOT NULL AND (("confirmedAt" IS NULL AND "cancelDisposition" = 'NOT_ALLOCATED') OR ("confirmedAt" IS NOT NULL AND "dispatchedAt" IS NULL AND "cancelDisposition" = 'RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE') OR ("dispatchedAt" IS NOT NULL AND "cancelDisposition" IN ('RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE','WRITTEN_OFF')))))`. State in Task 7 that PLACED stores NOT_ALLOCATED and CONFIRMED stores RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE (system-set). Add Step 4 tests for NOT_ALLOCATED with dispatchedAt set (rejected) and for a disposition on a non-cancelled order (rejected).

title: No CHECK ties qtyUnitsRequested to qtyBoxesRequested x unitsPerBoxSnapshot, so a box/unit mix-up allocates the wrong quantity silently
failure_scenario: Task 4 (placement) or Task 5 (admin edit `{ orderLineId, qtyBoxes }`) might write `qtyUnitsRequested: qtyBoxes` without boxesToUnits, or update boxes without units. With unitsPerBox 100, an order for 5 boxes requests 5 units. allocate takes 5 units, fulfilled == requested, and it looks like a complete fulfilment. The existing CHECK (`fulfilled BETWEEN 0 AND requested`) passes, and none of the listed Task 4/5 tests compares units to boxes. Fixtures that use unitsPerBox = 1 hide it completely.
fix: Add to the hand-written migration: `ALTER TABLE "order_lines" ADD CONSTRAINT "order_lines_units_match_boxes" CHECK ("qtyBoxesRequested" > 0 AND "unitsPerBoxSnapshot" > 0 AND "qtyUnitsRequested" = "qtyBoxesRequested" * "unitsPerBoxSnapshot" AND "pricePerBoxSnapshot" >= 0 AND "lineTotal" >= 0);` and `ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "orders_total_non_negative" CHECK ("totalAmount" >= 0);`. Add matching Step 4 tests. Also test the boundary value 0 for cart_lines, not just a negative, since Task 3's PATCH-to-0 semantics depend on it.

location: Task 1, Step 4 (line 303: 'Add to test/integration/search-normalisation.spec.ts's constraint block ...') and Task 2's spec, which has no setup/cleanup shown. The models rely on default onDelete for Order.client, OrderLine.item, CartLine.item, ClientInventoryItem.item, OrderLineAllocation.batch and ClientBatchHolding.batch.
title: New RESTRICT foreign keys break every existing suite's deleteMany cleanup, including the block Step 4 extends
failure_scenario: Required relations without onDelete are emitted as ON DELETE RESTRICT, as with items_categoryId_fkey in the catalog migration. The 'qtyUnitsFulfilled above requested' test has to insert a valid order first, and that row survives. The constraint block's next beforeEach runs `prisma.user.deleteMany()`, which fails with P2003 (orders_clientId_fkey), and the rest of the block fails along with its afterAll. Allocation-spec rows (orders, lines, allocations) left behind make `warehouseBatch.deleteMany()` / `item.deleteMany()` / `user.deleteMany()` in batches, items, categories, admin-users and the other e2e suites fail. The suites share one database with fileParallelism: false, and Vitest's default sequencer orders files by cached duration and size, not by name, so the breakage is order-dependent and flaky. Assertions like `toHaveLength(1)` in the ORDER_OUT test also depend on per-test cleanup, which the plan never specifies.
fix: Add a Task 1 step that creates `test/helpers/reset-db.ts`, which runs `TRUNCATE` on all application tables (everything except `_prisma_migrations`) with `RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE`, and switch every existing suite's beforeEach/afterAll to it. If that is too broad, list the FK-safe delete order explicitly (orderLineAllocation, orderLine, order, cartLine, cart, clientBatchHolding, clientInventoryItem, hotDealEntry, then the existing chain) and apply it to all suites in the same commit. Spell out the allocation spec's beforeEach and the `seedBatch`/`allocateInTx`/`confirmAnOrderFor` helpers.

location: Task 2, Step 3, `const minShelfLifeDays = await this.settings.get(...)` inside allocate (line 506). The header's Consumes table (lines 50-51) gives SettingsService.get and AuditService.record without a transaction parameter, and Task 5 (line 680) says 'One transaction: ... audit'.
title: In-transaction calls to services bound to the root PrismaService use a second pooled connection (pool starvation; audit committed outside the tx)
failure_scenario: SettingsService.get and AuditService.record use `this.prisma`, not `tx`. Each in-flight confirmation holds one pool connection for its transaction and then asks for another. PrismaPg built from a connection string uses a pg.Pool with the default max of 10 and connectionTimeoutMillis of 0. With 10 concurrent confirmations, every transaction waits forever for an 11th connection until Prisma's 5 s timeout rolls all of them back (P2028). An audit written inside Task 5's callback commits on its own connection. If the confirmation then rolls back (the plan's own 'a failed line rolls back the entire confirmation' case), the audit log says ORDER_CONFIRMED for an order that is still PLACED. BatchesService.receive deliberately audits after commit.
fix: Resolve settings before opening the transaction and pass the result in: `opts: { orderId, actorUserId, minShelfLifeDays }`, or better a precomputed business-date cutoff string bound as `${cutoff}::date`. Record the audit after `$transaction` resolves (the existing pattern), or give AuditService.record an optional `tx` parameter. Update the Consumes table to match.

location: Task 2, Step 3, `AND "qtyUnitsRemaining" > 0` in the locking SELECT (line 523).
title: Filtering qty > 0 before locking lets a confirmation that raced a release skip a batch the release just refilled (FEFO anomaly)
failure_scenario: Under READ COMMITTED, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE re-checks only rows that qualified in its statement snapshot. Rows that start qualifying because of the transaction it waited on are never seen. An order's allocations naturally drain EARLY to 0 and take part of MID. Cancel that order: release tx C restores EARLY 0 -> 200 and MID 50 -> 150. Meanwhile confirmation B for the same item takes its snapshot, where EARLY (qty 0) is filtered out, MID is a candidate and C holds it. B waits on MID, and after C commits it re-reads MID = 150 and allocates from it. EARLY, which expires first and now holds 200, is skipped. B has seen C's write to MID but not to EARLY, which is not serializable. A later-expiring batch ships, EARLY ages on the shelf, and nothing reports it.
fix: Drop `"qtyUnitsRemaining" > 0` from the WHERE clause, so zero-stock batches inside the shelf-life window are also locked. The existing `if (take <= 0) continue` already skips them. B then waits on EARLY as well, because C holds it, and re-reads it at 200. The extra locks are bounded by the `expiryDate > cutoff` window.

title: release() deletes allocations but leaves OrderLine.qtyUnitsFulfilled (and the fulfilled-based totalAmount) claiming the stock was supplied
failure_scenario: After a CONFIRMED cancel, or an OUT_FOR_DELIVERY RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE cancel, the lines still show qtyUnitsFulfilled = 200 and totalAmount still bills for it, but no allocation rows exist. The invariant SUM(allocations) == qtyUnitsFulfilled that Task 6 and Task 11 rely on ('requested vs fulfilled', 'the FEFO allocation with batch numbers') no longer holds. Any report or dashboard that sums fulfilled units or totals without filtering on status counts cancelled orders. For a returned shipment, the admin detail screen can no longer show which batches physically went out and came back. That link now survives only as orderId-level stock_movements.
fix: Either keep the rows and add `releasedAt DateTime?` to OrderLineAllocation (release sets it, and delivery and allocation reads filter on `releasedAt: null`), or have release also run `tx.orderLine.updateMany({ where: { orderId }, data: { qtyUnitsFulfilled: 0 } })` and state in the plan that a cancelled order's totalAmount is historical. Add an assertion to the Task 2 release test for whichever is chosen.
